prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

PARIS, France (CNN) -- Hundreds of French workers, angry about proposed layoffs at a Caterpillar factory, were holding executives of the company hostage Tuesday, a spokesman for the workers said. Caterpillar's French staff say they are angry about a lack of negotiations over layoffs. It is at least the third time this month that French workers threatened with cutbacks have blockaded managers in their offices to demand negotiations. Executives were released unharmed in both previous situations. The latest incident started Tuesday morning at the office of the construction equipment company in the southeastern city of Grenoble. The workers were angry that Caterpillar had proposed cutting more than 700 jobs and would not negotiate, said Nicolas Benoit, a spokesman for the workers' union. They did not want to harm the Caterpillar executives, Benoit told CNN. One hostage was released Tuesday evening leaving workers with four captives inside the Caterpillar building. The released man was a human resources director identified only as Mr. Petit, because he has heart problems, union representative Bernard Patrick told CNN. Petit had a heart attack a few weeks ago, Patrick said. The four others still being held are Nicolas Polutnik, the head of operations; two other executives; and Petit's personal assistant, he said. About 500 employees were also outside the building protesting. A top Caterpillar executive called the hostage-taking unhelpful. "The actions that are taking place today, led by a small minority of individuals, are not helping as we work for a positive resolution of this situation," said Chris Schena, Caterpillar vice president with responsibility for manufacturing operations in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, in a statement. "The best way to resolve this matter is to continue the negotiations through the Works Council to find a solution that's fair to our employees and allows Caterpillar to remain a leader in a rapidly changing global marketplace," Schena said, adding that the company was "concerned for the safety of our employees." Benoit said all the workers wanted to do was negotiate with Caterpillar and they were upset that the company did not show up to two earlier scheduled negotiating sessions. The employees being held in their office were being allowed to get food, Benoit added. Police arrived at the scene two hours after the incident began but it had not been settled. Employees at a French 3M factory held a manager hostage for more than 24 hours Wednesday and Thursday of last week over a dispute about terms for laid-off staff. Luc Rousselet, who was unharmed, was allowed to leave the plant in Pithiviers, central France, early on Thursday morning after talks between unions and officials from 3M France. Earlier this month, the boss of Sony France was held overnight before workers freed him after he agreed to reopen talks on compensation when the factory closed. France has been hit by nationwide strikes twice in the past two months.

PARIS, France (CNN) — Hundreds of French workers, angered by proposed layoffs at a Caterpillar factory, were holding company executives hostage on Tuesday, according to a spokesman for the workers.

Caterpillar’s French employees say they are frustrated by what they describe as a lack of negotiations over the planned job cuts. It is at least the third time this month that French workers facing cutbacks have blockaded managers in their offices to demand talks. In both previous cases, the executives were released unharmed.

The latest incident began Tuesday morning at the construction equipment company’s office in Grenoble, a city in southeastern France. Workers were angered by Caterpillar’s proposal to cut more than 700 jobs and by what they said was the company’s refusal to negotiate, said Nicolas Benoit, a spokesman for the workers’ union.

Benoit told CNN that the workers did not intend to harm the Caterpillar executives.

One hostage was released Tuesday evening, leaving workers with four captives inside the Caterpillar building. The man released was a human resources director identified only as Mr. Petit, who was freed because he has heart problems, union representative Bernard Patrick told CNN. Petit had suffered a heart attack a few weeks earlier, Patrick said.

The four people still being held were Nicolas Polutnik, the head of operations; two other executives; and Petit’s personal assistant, Patrick said. About 500 employees were also protesting outside the building.

A senior Caterpillar executive described the hostage-taking as unhelpful.

“The actions that are taking place today, led by a small minority of individuals, are not helping as we work for a positive resolution of this situation,” Chris Schena, Caterpillar vice president responsible for manufacturing operations in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, said in a statement.

“The best way to resolve this matter is to continue the negotiations through the Works Council to find a solution that’s fair to our employees and allows Caterpillar to remain a leader in a rapidly changing global marketplace,” Schena said, adding that the company was “concerned for the safety of our employees.”

Benoit said the workers’ sole aim was to negotiate with Caterpillar, and that they were upset because the company had failed to attend two previously scheduled negotiating sessions. He added that the employees being held in their office were being allowed to obtain food.

Police arrived at the scene two hours after the incident began, but the standoff had not been resolved.

The confrontation followed similar incidents in France. Employees at a French 3M factory held a manager hostage for more than 24 hours on Wednesday and Thursday of the previous week amid a dispute over terms for laid-off staff. Luc Rousselet, who was unharmed, was allowed to leave the plant in Pithiviers, central France, early Thursday morning after talks between unions and officials from 3M France.

Earlier this month, the head of Sony France was held overnight before workers freed him after he agreed to reopen talks on compensation related to the factory’s closure.

France has been hit by nationwide strikes twice in the past two months.

Caterpillar employees in France said their frustration stemmed from what they described as the company’s refusal to negotiate over layoffs. The episode marked at least the third time this month that French workers facing cutbacks had confined managers in their offices in an effort to force talks. In the two earlier cases, the executives were freed without injury.

The latest standoff began Tuesday morning at Caterpillar’s construction-equipment offices in Grenoble, a city in southeastern France. Nicolas Benoit, a union spokesman, said workers were upset because Caterpillar had proposed eliminating more than 700 positions and was unwilling to bargain. Benoit told CNN the workers had no intention of hurting the Caterpillar executives.

By Tuesday evening, one of the people being held had been released, leaving four others inside the Caterpillar building. Union representative Bernard Patrick told CNN the man released was a human resources director identified only as Mr. Petit, who was let go because he has heart problems. Patrick said Petit had suffered a heart attack several weeks earlier.

According to Patrick, those still being detained were Nicolas Polutnik, the company’s head of operations; two additional executives; and Petit’s personal assistant. Around 500 employees were also gathered outside the building in protest.

A senior Caterpillar official criticized the detention, saying it did not help resolve the dispute. “The actions that are taking place today, led by a small minority of individuals, are not helping as we work for a positive resolution of this situation,” Chris Schena, Caterpillar vice president responsible for manufacturing operations in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, said in a statement.

Schena said the proper path forward was to keep negotiating through the Works Council in order to reach an outcome that was fair to employees while enabling Caterpillar to remain competitive in a quickly changing global market. He added that the company was concerned about employee safety.

Benoit said the workers’ goal was simply to secure negotiations with Caterpillar. He said they were angry because the company had failed to attend two previously scheduled bargaining sessions. He also said the employees confined in the office were being permitted to obtain food.

Police reached the site about two hours after the incident began, but the situation had not yet been resolved.

The Caterpillar incident followed similar labor actions in France. The previous week, employees at a French 3M plant held a manager for more than 24 hours, from Wednesday into Thursday, during a dispute over conditions for laid-off workers. The manager, Luc Rousselet, was not harmed and was allowed to leave the factory in Pithiviers, in central France, early Thursday after discussions between unions and 3M France officials.

Earlier in the month, workers held the head of Sony France overnight and released him only after he agreed to resume negotiations over compensation tied to a factory closure.

France has also experienced nationwide strikes twice during the past two months.

Union representatives said the action at the Grenoble-area site was intended to force management back to the negotiating table after the U.S.-based heavy equipment maker announced proposed layoffs affecting its French operations.

“We recognize the anxiety caused by the proposed restructuring, but holding managers against their will is unacceptable,” a company spokesperson said. “Caterpillar remains committed to dialogue with employee representatives and to finding solutions within the framework of the law.”

French officials urged both sides to resume talks and bring the standoff to a peaceful end. Labor Ministry representatives were expected to monitor negotiations as local authorities remained near the site.

Workers said they feared the layoffs would devastate the Grenoble region, where Caterpillar has long been a major industrial employer.

“They ask us for sacrifices when things are difficult, but when the company makes profits, workers are forgotten,” another union official said. “If Caterpillar wants to cut jobs, it must put serious compensation and redeployment measures on the table.”

The confrontation reflects broader unrest across France as companies restructure in response to the global recession. Unions have accused multinational firms of using the crisis to reduce payrolls, while employers argue that falling orders have left them with few options.

Negotiations between union leaders and Caterpillar management were expected to continue, with workers insisting the executives would not be released until they received stronger guarantees on severance, job protections and future investment at the site.
